name: Candid on AI in Nonprofits: Ethics, Grants and Adoption Research
title: Candid on AI in Nonprofits: Ethics, Grants and Adoption Research
answer: Candid's website collects blog articles and guidance on artificial intelligence in the social sector, covering ethical use, funder attitudes toward AI-generated grant applications, nonprofit adoption and funding needs. Its most useful single finding comes from Candid's annual survey of foundation giving trends: 57% of grantmakers do not know whether they have received applications created with generative AI, 67% are undecided about accepting them, and only 10% accept them. The pages also document Candid's own work to correct bias in its grants auto-coding system and to publish model cards for its AI tools.

sections.body: Candid publishes these pages on candid.org as a collection of blog articles, guidance and research summaries about AI in the social sector. The pages include a Candid data science manager's article on ethical AI tools, a Candid annual survey analysis of foundation giving trends and AI-generated applications, a tips page gathering resources from Candid and external commentators, an April 08, 2026 article on nonprofit AI needs, and a summary of a Blackbaud Institute report on AI impact and donor trust. The scope is nonprofit and foundation practice, not a single formal report.
sections.heading: What this source is

sections.body: Candid's data science manager writes that AI tools are trained on mostly human-generated data and often amplify bias. Candid's grants auto-coding system, which predicts Philanthropy Classification System codes and codes most grants data in Candid products, once predicted that grants serving low-income populations also served People of African Descent, and associated People of Latin American descent with incarcerated people. Candid addressed this through data investigations, corrections, changes to sampling, and continued refinement of training and evaluation data. The article recommends defining bias and harm for each use case, establishing evaluation procedures, verifying AI outputs, and producing model cards. Candid has AI policies for staff and produces model cards for all AI tools it builds and deploys. A separate Candid survey found 57% of grantmakers do not know if they have received AI-generated applications, 42% believe they have not, under 1% said they have, 10% accept them, 23% would not, and 67% are undecided. Other pages report that 84% of AI-powered nonprofits need funding to scale, 62% of foundation and nonprofit leaders say few staff understand AI, 90% of nonprofit leaders want to use AI more, and only 17% say funders have engaged them on AI. A Blackbaud Institute summary says one in 10 nonprofits are AI-adaptive, nearly four in 10 are merely aware, and AI saves staff time, $503 per employee per week on average, or $621 at AI-adaptive organizations.
sections.heading: What it says

sections.body: Candid's annual survey of foundation giving trends reports 57% of grantmakers do not know whether they have received AI-generated applications, 42% believe they have not, under 1% said they have, 10% accept AI-generated applications, 23% would not accept them, and 67% are undecided. Candid's data science manager describes the grants auto-coding system's bias examples and says Candid produces model cards for all AI tools it builds and deploys. Fast Forward's 2025 AI for Humanity Report found 84% of AI-powered nonprofit respondents need funding to scale AI-enabled solutions, and 71% have processes to assess and mitigate AI risks. A Center for Effective Philanthropy survey found 62% of foundation and nonprofit leaders said none or just a few staff have a solid understanding of AI, 90% of nonprofit leaders want to use AI more, and 17% said funders have engaged them on AI. The Blackbaud Institute report categorized one in 10 nonprofits as AI-adaptive and nearly four in 10 as aware. AI-adaptive nonprofits were more likely to see increased overall revenue at 75%, improved fundraising revenue at 64%, and strengthened donor retention at 48%. AI saves staff time, $503 per employee per week on average, and $621 at AI-adaptive organizations. The report found 85% used AI at work but only 33% said their organization used it very effectively, only half had paid or enterprise versions, and nearly a quarter used free versions.
sections.heading: Figures and claims worth noting

sections.body: A reader following AI in nonprofits would use this source to understand the gap between interest and readiness. It gives funder-side data on whether AI-generated applications are accepted, nonprofit-side data on funding and skills shortages, and a candid account of bias in a grants auto-coding system that classifies sector data. It also offers practical positions on evaluation, model cards, staff policies, inclusive adoption, and human-centered use. The pages are useful for benchmarking adoption, donor trust, and responsible AI practices, and for seeing where philanthropic capital is needed before impact can be demonstrated.
sections.heading: What it means for AI in Nonprofits

sections.body: This is a collection of blog articles, guidance and summaries rather than a single comprehensive report. Several findings come from external surveys, including Salesforce, Fast Forward, the Center for Effective Philanthropy and the Blackbaud Institute, and the pages do not include their full methodologies. Only one article is dated in the findings, April 08, 2026. The pages focus on Candid's perspective and curated resources, so they do not provide detailed technical implementation, legal compliance guidance, or a complete picture of every nonprofit subsector.
